quals-wisconsin-algebra-2011f-01.prompt:
Let $p$ be a fixed prime number and let $G$ be a finite group. A normal subgroup $K$ of $G$ is said to be a "normal $p$-complement" if $p\nmid|K|$ and $|G : K|$ is a power of $p$.

(a) If $G$ has a normal $p$-complement and $H$ is a subgroup of $G$, show that $H$ has a normal $p$-complement.

(b) If $G$ has a normal $p$-complement and $N$ is a normal subgroup of $G$, show that $G/N$ has a normal $p$-complement.

(c) Let $U$ and $V$ be normal subgroups of $G$, and suppose both $U$ and $V$ have normal $p$-complements. Prove that $UV$ has a normal $p$-complement.
quals-wisconsin-algebra-2011f-01.answer: (a) $H\cap K$, since $|H:H\cap K|=|HK:K|$ divides $|G:K|$. (b) $KN/N$. (c) A normal $p$-complement is the set of all $p'$-elements, hence characteristic; so $K_UK_V\trianglelefteq G$ is a $p'$-group, and $UV/K_UK_V$ is a product of two normal $p$-subgroups.

quals-wisconsin-algebra-2011f-02.prompt:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring with $1$ and let $Q$ be a primary ideal of $R$. Suppose $a\in R$ with $a\notin Q$ and define $I = \{ r\in R \mid ar\in Q\}$ so that $I$ is an ideal of $R$.

(a) Show that $\sqrt I = \sqrt Q$.

(b) Prove that $I$ is a primary ideal of $R$.

(c) If $R$ is noetherian, show that the element $a$ can be chosen so that $I$ is a prime ideal.
quals-wisconsin-algebra-2011f-02.answer:
(a) $Q\subseteq I$, and $r^k\in I$ means $ar^k\in Q$ with $a
otin Q$, so $r\in\sqrt Q$. (b) $xy\in I$, $x
otin I$: $(ax)y\in Q$ with $ax
otin Q$, so $y\in\sqrt Q=\sqrt I$. (c) Choose $(Q:a)$ maximal among the proper ideals $(Q:a)$, $a
otin Q$; it is prime. (Or: with $P=\sqrt Q$ and $k$ minimal with $P^k\subseteq Q$, take $a\in P^{k-1}\setminus Q$; then $(Q:a)=P$.)

quals-wisconsin-algebra-2011f-03.prompt:
Let $K\subseteq F\subseteq E$ be fields with $E = F[\alpha]$ and with $\alpha^n\in F$ for some positive integer $n$. Suppose $K$ contains a primitive $n$th root of unity and let $L$ be a field with $K\subseteq L\subseteq E$ and $L\cap F = K$.

(a) If $L$ is Galois over $K$, show that $L = K[\beta]$ for some element $\beta$ with $\beta^n\in K$.

(b) Show by example that $L$ need not be Galois over $K$. (Hint. Take $n = 2$.)
quals-wisconsin-algebra-2011f-03.answer: (a) $E/F$ is cyclic Kummer of degree dividing $n$; by natural irrationalities $\mathrm{Gal}(L/K)\cong\mathrm{Gal}(LF/F)$, a quotient of $\mathrm{Gal}(E/F)$, so $L/K$ is cyclic of degree $m\mid n$ and Kummer theory gives $L=K(\beta)$, $\beta^m\in K$. (b) $K=\mathbb Q$, $F=\mathbb Q(\omega\sqrt[3]2)$, $\alpha=\sqrt{-3}$, $E=\mathbb Q(\sqrt[3]2,\omega)$, $L=\mathbb Q(\sqrt[3]2)$.

quals-wisconsin-algebra-2011f-04.prompt:
Let $n$ be a positive integer and let $V$ be an $n$-dimensional vector space over the field $K$. Let $m$ be a second positive integer and write $V^m = V\times V\times\cdots\times V$ ($m$ times). A "multilinear, alternating" function $f\colon V^m\to K$ is a function $f(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_m)$ which is multilinear, that is linear in each of the $m$ variables $x_i\in V$, and alternating, that is $f(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_m) = 0$ if any two of the variables are equal.

(a) Prove that the set $S$ of all multilinear, alternating functions from $V^m$ to $K$ is naturally a $K$-vector space and that $S = 0$ if $m > n$.

(b) If $m\le n$, prove that $\dim_K S$ is bounded above by the binomial coefficient $\binom nm$ and that $\dim_K S = 1$ when $m = n$.
quals-wisconsin-algebra-2011f-04.answer: Alternating forms are antisymmetric and vanish on linearly dependent tuples, so (a) $S=0$ for $m>n$; (b) $f$ is determined by its values $f(e_{i_1},\dots,e_{i_m})$ on increasing index tuples, giving an injection $S\hookrightarrow K^{\binom nm}$, and for $m=n$ the determinant is a nonzero element.

quals-wisconsin-algebra-2011f-05.prompt:
Let $A$ be an additive abelian group. We say that $A$ is "free abelian" if it has a subset (possibly infinite) $\mathcal B = \{ b_i \mid i\in\mathcal I\}$ such that every element $a\in A$ is uniquely writable as a finite sum $a = \sum_{i\in\mathcal I} n_ib_i$ where each $n_i\in\mathbb Z$ is an integer. Next, we say that $a\in A$ is a "divisible element" if for each integer $n > 0$ there exists $a_n\in A$ with $na_n = a$.

(a) If $A$ is free abelian, prove that $A$ contains no nonzero divisible element.

(b) Let $A = \prod\mathbb Z$ be the unrestricted direct product of countably many copies of the additive abelian group $\mathbb Z$. Thus $A$ is the set of all countably infinite tuples of elements of the integers $\mathbb Z$. Let $B$ be the subgroup of $A$ which is the restricted direct product. Thus $B$ is the set of all countably infinite tuples of elements of $\mathbb Z$ with almost all entries equal to $0$. Prove that $A/B$ contains a nonzero divisible element and conclude that $A/B$ is not free abelian.
quals-wisconsin-algebra-2011f-05.answer: (a) If $a=\sum n_ib_i$ with $n_j\neq0$ and $a=Na_N$, uniqueness gives $N\mid n_j$ for every $N$, impossible for $N>|n_j|$. (b) $x=(1!,2!,3!,\dots)+B$ is nonzero and divisible: for $n>0$, $y=(0,\dots,0,n!/n,(n+1)!/n,\dots)$ has $ny-x\in B$.
